assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: full life cycle
items.clue: Every stage from obtaining raw materials to disposal.

items.label: global climate change
items.clue: A long-term shift in weather patterns, driven mainly by a rise in average temperature.

items.label: carbon footprint
items.clue: The total greenhouse gases emitted over the whole existence of a product, service or event.

items.label: Incomplete combustion
items.clue: Burning in a limited supply of air, so that some carbon is only partly oxidised to carbon monoxide or is released as solid carbon (soot), and some hydrocarbon may pass through unburned.

questions.stem: Radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the ground. What happens next?

options.text: The ground reflects the radiation back at the same wavelength.
The warmed surface emits longer wavelength radiation.
The surface emits radiation of an even shorter wavelength.
The warm air rises and is trapped by greenhouse gases.

questions.explanation: The Earth's surface, being much cooler than the Sun, radiates at longer wavelengths.

questions.stem: A student is asked to name two human activities that increase the amount of carbon dioxide. Which pair is correct?

options.text: Burning fossil fuels for electricity, and deforestation.
Cattle farming, and decay of waste in landfill sites.
Burning fossil fuels, and keeping herds of cattle.
Deforestation, and the melting of the polar ice.

questions.explanation: These are the two carbon dioxide activities named in the specification.

questions.stem: A report says that the risk to a coastal city from climate change is high. What does describing the risk involve?

options.text: How severe the flooding would be, however unlikely it is.
How many people believe that the report is correct.
How likely the flooding is, and how severe it would be.
How likely the flooding is, however small the damage.

questions.explanation: Risk combines the chance of an event with the size of its consequences.

questions.stem: Which action would reduce emissions of methane?

options.text: Bury much more waste in landfill so that the gas cannot escape.
Fit filters to the power station chimneys to trap the methane.
Collect the gas from landfill sites and burn it as a fuel.
Burn less coal in the power stations that are nearby.

questions.explanation: Capturing the gas stops methane escaping into the atmosphere, and it is put to use as a fuel.

questions.stem: What do greenhouse gases do with the long wavelength radiation they absorb?

options.text: They re-radiate it in all directions, including back towards the Earth.
They reflect all of it straight back down to the Earth's surface.
They store it permanently, so the energy never leaves the gas.
They convert it into short wavelength radiation from the Sun.

questions.explanation: Absorption is followed by re-radiation, and the part sent downwards keeps the surface warm.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes what scientists say about human activity and the Earth's temperature?

options.text: Scientists have now proved that human activity is the only possible cause of warming.
Scientists disagree with each other, so there is no reliable evidence at all.
The claim comes from opinions in the media rather than from measured data.
Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists expect the Earth's surface to warm.

questions.explanation: This is the specification's own statement of the scientific position.

questions.stem: Give one reason why actions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions may be limited.

options.text: There is no evidence for the warming.
Alternative technologies cost a lot.
Emissions cannot be measured at all today.
The evidence has not yet been peer reviewed.

questions.explanation: Cost is a named reason why action is limited.

questions.stem: Why do different climate models give different predictions for future temperatures?

options.text: Climate models are built on opinion rather than on any real measured data.
The temperature of the whole of the atmosphere cannot be measured well.
Global climate is a very complex system, so models must be simplified.
The results of the models have not been checked by peer review.

questions.explanation: The specification says such complex systems are difficult to model, which leads to simplified models.

questions.stem: A newspaper article about climate change is described as biased. What does this mean?

options.text: Its thermometers were badly calibrated.
It presents only part of the evidence.
It disagrees with peer-reviewed research.
Its writer is uncertain about the outcome.

questions.explanation: Bias here is selective use of evidence, or opinion presented as evidence.

questions.stem: A website claims that the world is cooling, using two years of readings from one weather station. What is the best evaluation of this evidence?

options.text: The sample is too small and the period too short to show a global trend.
The evidence is strong because real temperatures were measured.
The evidence is worthless because a website is not a journal.
Two years is enough if the thermometer was accurate enough.

questions.explanation: A global, long-term claim needs data from many places over many years.

questions.stem: Which of these is a genuine uncertainty in the evidence base for global climate change?

options.text: Nobody had measured the temperature of the Earth before the year 2000.
Scientists made mistakes when they recorded their measurements.
It is not known whether carbon dioxide absorbs radiation.
Future emissions are not known, so predictions are given as a range.

questions.explanation: What humans will emit in future is a real unknown, so models give ranges.

questions.stem: Why is peer review of climate research important?

options.text: It proves that the conclusions are right and settles the matter for good.
It lets the general public vote on which scientific results to believe.
Other scientists check the methods and conclusions before publication.
It checks that the thermometers were properly calibrated.

questions.explanation: Peer review is checking by other scientists in the same field.
